statement: In the studies read, a test that showed one drug did not show what else was in the sample or how much drug it held, and no study measured whether a negative result means a sample is less risky. A colour kit read by experienced analysts gave the same positive MDMA reading for seven samples that also held caffeine, ephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA as for samples of MDMA alone (Murray et al., 2003). In drug-checking samples in the Vancouver area, 24 of 159 contained a newer benzodiazepine that the person had not expected (most expected fentanyl), 17 of them also held fentanyl, and infrared spectroscopy, which can identify several components, listed fentanyl in only 3 of those 17 and a benzodiazepine in 2 of the 24 (editors' count from the paper's table; Laing et al., 2021). Each strip type reacts to one drug or family and missed related drugs in laboratory tests: xylazine strips did not react to medetomidine or several other sedatives (Sisco et al., 2024a), and nitazene, fentanyl and benzodiazepine strips missed some nitazenes, fentanyl analogues and etizolam (see the answers on each strip). Fentanyl strips are built to show presence only, not concentration, purity or which analogue (Green et al., 2020); in pure solutions the test band became fainter as the fentanyl concentration rose, but the makers' rule reads only whether a band is there (Bergh et al., 2021), no study read tested whether a line's strength shows how much drug a sample holds, and a scoping review lists that belief among mistaken ones (Kutscher et al., 2024, second-hand). Authors of three studies state that a negative result does not mean a drug is safe and that a positive one gives no amount (De Vrieze et al., 2024; Sisco et al., 2024a; Winstock et al., 2001); these are their conclusions, not tested findings. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: A test for one drug shows only that drug or its close relatives. In one laboratory study, MDMA samples with caffeine or amphetamine mixed in looked the same on a colour test as pure MDMA; at one drug-checking service, newer benzodiazepines turned up in samples people thought were fentanyl. Fentanyl strips show only whether fentanyl is there, not how much. No study tested whether a negative result makes a drug less risky.
population: Drug samples in the studies read: seized ecstasy samples tested in a laboratory, drug-checking samples at harm-reduction sites in one Canadian urban area, and prepared solutions
exposure: Single-target tests (colour reagents for MDMA; fentanyl, xylazine, nitazene and benzodiazepine strips) and FTIR
comparator: Laboratory analysis of the same samples (GC-MS, LC-MS or qNMR) or known content
outcome: Whether a reading showed other drugs present, how much drug a sample held, or whether a sample was less risky
magnitude: Murray et al.: 7 of 35 MDMA samples held a second drug, all read like MDMA alone. Laing et al.: 24/159 samples held an NPS benzodiazepine (15.1%), none expected; 17 of 24 also held fentanyl; FTIR listed fentanyl in 3 of those 17 and an NPS benzodiazepine in 2 of 24 (editors' count from Table 2). Sisco et al. (2024a): medetomidine and four α2-agonists did not react at 100 µg/mL. Amount: no study read tested whether strips or colour tests estimate amount.

evidence.extracted: All 35 samples with MDMA were read positive by every analyst, including seven that GC-MS showed also held caffeine (2), ephedrine (2), amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA; the readings did not set these apart from MDMA alone.

evidence.locator: Results › NPS benzodiazepines and opioids, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Tables 1 and 2 (p. 5)
evidence.extracted: Of 159 samples with point-of-care and confirmatory results, 24 (15.1%) contained an NPS benzodiazepine, none expected to by the person (15 were expected to be fentanyl, 5 alprazolam); 17 of the 24 also contained fentanyl (one also carfentanil), and several also held methamphetamine or phenacetin. Editors' count from Table 2: FTIR listed fentanyl (once as fentanyl or analogue) in 3 of the 17 samples in which the laboratory found fentanyl, and an NPS benzodiazepine in 2 of the 24.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Laing_2021_BenzoTestStrips.pdf (article-in-press version; pages as printed in it)

evidence.extracted: Xylazine strips did not react to medetomidine or the other α2-agonists in the panel, which would therefore not be detected, potentially creating a false sense of safety (authors); the authors call for comprehensive drug-checking services that identify a range of substances.

evidence.locator: Methods › Devices tested, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 5)
evidence.extracted: The strip does not measure fentanyl concentration and does not tell fentanyl apart from its analogues; it only shows whether fentanyl is present, and gives no information on quantity, purity, adulterants or fill.

evidence.locator: Results › Interpretation of test results, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: The makers' instructions call a test negative whenever two bands appear, whatever the intensity of the test band; with fentanyl at 10–250 ng/mL the results were highly concentration dependent, which led the authors to grade faint bands.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Fentanyl-and-analogues/Bergh_2021_FTS_SelectivitySensitivity.pdf (no printed page numbers; PDF pages)

evidence.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use › Ease of use, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Relays, as misinformation reported in the included studies, the belief that the intensity of the test indicates the purity of fentanyl in the supply, and that a negative fentanyl strip indicates xylazine (references 10, 30 and 48).
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Kutscher_2024_FTSScopingReview.pdf (PubMed Central author manuscript; AM p. = PDF page)

evidence.extracted: The authors state that a negative result does not imply that a sample is safe, since it may still contain non-reacting nitazenes, other synthetic opioids, other drugs or adulterants, and that a positive result gives no information on the identity, quantity or purity of the nitazene present.
evidence.source_read: publisher full text (HTML), https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12954-024-01078-8 (copy saved by AI reader 138, searched by AI reader 139)

evidence.locator: The usefulness of pill testing, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors state that colour tests give no indication that many harmful substances may be present in a pill, that knowing a pill contains MDMA does not show its effect until after it is taken, and that colour tests give no information on a pill's strength.

risk_of_bias.note: QUADAS-2 high for Murray et al. (selected evidence samples, readers who knew they were sold as MDMA); Laing et al.'s samples were selected and partially verified (high risk of bias on the card).

inconsistency.note: The tested findings point the same way.

indirectness.note: A 2003 colour kit read in a laboratory and one drug-checking programme's samples read by staff; the claim is about tests in general and at home.

imprecision.note: Seven samples with a second drug and 17 samples with fentanyl and an NPS benzodiazepine.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources; laboratory evaluations of test strips are not registered.

grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence starts high and is rated down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, so very low. Rated as worded: what these tests showed and did not show in these studies. The statements about amount and safety are design facts of the devices and authors' conclusions, labelled as such; no study read tested whether a negative result is linked to less harm. Status replicated: Murray et al. and Laing et al. are independent and point the same way.
